title: Disaster from the North
summary: God's invitation to return comes with conditions: put away idols, swear by the LORD in truth and justice, break up the hard ground, and circumcise the heart. Then the alarm sounds. A lion has left its thicket, a destroyer of nations is on the march, and a scorching wind is blowing from the desert. Jeremiah cries out in anguish, sees the land undone as if creation had been reversed, and hears Zion gasp like a woman in labor before her killers.
story: Chapter 3 ended with a people confessing their sins. Chapter 4 answers that repentance must be real: not words, but a changed heart and a changed life. When the call to return has been made, the book turns abruptly to what will happen if it is refused. This is the first full picture of the enemy from the north announced in Jeremiah's call (1:13-15). The invader is not yet named; he is a lion, a storm, a wind, horses swifter than eagles. From here to the end of chapter 6 the alarm keeps sounding, and the reader watches a nation hear it and refuse to move.
historical:
The foe from the north in chapters 4 to 6 is never named in these chapters. Some older scholars, drawing on the Greek historian Herodotus, suggested that Jeremiah first had in mind Scythian raiders from the steppes, who were active in the Near East in the seventh century BC. Most scholars today think the prophet meant Babylon from the start or that these poems came to be understood of Babylon once its army appeared; 25:9 explicitly identifies the northern peoples with Nebuchadnezzar. Babylon lay to the east, but its armies reached Judah by the northern road through Syria, so they arrived from the north.

Verse 15 traces the enemy's advance. Dan, at the source of the Jordan, was Israel's northernmost town, and the hill country of Ephraim lies just north of Jerusalem. A message sent from Dan and then from Ephraim pictures the invader moving south, stage by stage, toward the capital. The final siege and fall came in 588 to 586 BC, but Judah had already felt Babylonian power in 605 and 597 BC.
cultural:
The ram's horn (shofar) was blown to warn of attack, and villagers in open country would flee to walled towns. A signal flag raised on a hill told people which way to run. Sackcloth, a coarse cloth of goat hair, was worn in mourning and in national emergencies. Verse 4 draws on circumcision, the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17): a physical mark meant to express belonging to God. Circumcising the heart meant removing whatever made the heart closed and unresponsive to God, an idea already in Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6.

The searing wind of verse 11 is the hot east wind (the sirocco) that blows off the desert in spring and autumn, withering plants. When farmers winnowed grain, they tossed it in a gentle breeze so the chaff blew away; this wind is too strong for winnowing, it flattens everything. Verse 30 describes a woman painting her eyes with kohl and putting on scarlet and gold to win lovers, an image for Judah trying to buy the favor of foreign powers who will turn on her.
literary: The chapter is mostly poetry and moves rapidly between voices: God, the prophet, the people, and a narrator describing the invasion. Sometimes it is hard to tell whether God or Jeremiah is speaking, and that blurring is part of the effect, since both grieve. Verses 19 to 21 are Jeremiah's own cry of anguish. Verses 23 to 26 are one of the most striking poems in the prophets: four times the prophet says I looked, and each time he sees creation undone. The earth is formless and void (the exact words of Genesis 1:2), the light is gone, the mountains shake, humans and birds have vanished, and the fruitful land is desert. It is Genesis 1 run backward. The chapter ends not with the prophet's voice but with Zion's, gasping in the pains of a birth that brings only death.

outline.t: Conditions for return: circumcise your hearts
Sound the alarm: the lion has left his thicket
A searing wind and a besieging army

doctrines.note: Repentance involves removing idols, speaking truly, and a changed heart. The images of breaking up fallow ground and circumcising the heart show that God wants inner renewal, not only outward religion. Even at this late stage the offer is real: wash your heart, so that you may be saved.

Judgment comes because of the people's ways and deeds, and it is felt as the undoing of creation itself. Yet God says he will not make a full end (verse 27), a small but important limit that the book repeats.

Jeremiah does not announce judgment coldly. He writhes in pain over what he sees. The prophet's grief reflects God's own, and it shows that faithful people may suffer deeply even when they know judgment is just.

words.note: Tohu, formlessness, paired here with bohu, void. The pair appears together only here, in Genesis 1:2, and in Isaiah 34:11. By using the exact words of Genesis 1:2, Jeremiah pictures judgment as a return to the state before God brought order. Sin does not only break laws; it unravels the world God made good.

Mul, to circumcise. Jeremiah calls the men of Judah to circumcise themselves to the LORD and remove the foreskins of their hearts. The physical rite was the covenant sign; the prophet insists that the sign means nothing without the reality, a heart opened to God. Paul takes up the same idea in Romans 2:28-29.

Shophar, the ram's horn trumpet, blown for alarm, for gathering the people, and at festivals. Its sound runs through this chapter (verses 5, 19, and 21): the prophet cannot stop hearing it. The trumpet that called Israel to worship now calls them to flee.

Meeh, the inner organs or belly, which Hebrew treated as the seat of deep emotion. Verse 19, translated My anguish, my anguish, literally reads My bowels, my bowels. The prophet's grief is physical, felt in his gut.

christ: The promise in verse 2 that the nations will be blessed through the LORD and glory in him echoes God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. Jeremiah links that blessing to Israel's faithful return; the New Testament sees it fulfilled when Christ, Abraham's offspring, brings the blessing to the nations (Galatians 3:8, 14). The call to circumcise the heart becomes a central theme in Paul, who says true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29; compare Colossians 2:11). And the picture of creation undone prepares for the Bible's answer: the God who could reverse creation in judgment will make a new creation, which the New Testament says has begun in the risen Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). These are connections drawn by the New Testament, not predictions in the chapter itself.

hard.q: In verse 10 Jeremiah says God has deceived the people by promising peace. Does God deceive?
hard.a:
The verse is startling: “Ah, Lord GOD, how completely You have deceived this people.” Interpreters take it in two main ways. Many read it as Jeremiah's anguished protest, not a doctrinal statement: in his shock he blames God for the false prophets' message of peace, which the book elsewhere says God never sent (14:13-15; 23:16-17). Others note that in Hebrew thought God is often described as the ultimate cause of what he permits, so that when people prefer lies, God can be said to give them over to their chosen deception (compare 1 Kings 22:19-23 and Paul in 2 Thessalonians 2:11).

What the book as a whole makes clear is that God did not send the prophets of peace; he sent Jeremiah to warn. The verse lets us hear the prophet's bewilderment honestly, and it prepares for his later confessions, where he goes further and accuses God of deceiving him (20:7).

questions: What would it mean for you to break up your unplowed ground and circumcise your heart? What has become hard or closed in you?
Jeremiah felt the coming disaster in his body before it arrived. What does his anguish teach about how to speak of judgment?
The poem of verses 23 to 26 pictures sin undoing creation. Where do you see the effects of human sin unraveling the goodness of the world?
